notes: Cross-arena multiplayer knowledge: aiming, movement, pickups, spawns, modes and weapon sets. Not tied to one stage, which is why it carries a leading underscore and is validated without level data.

This is the layer that separates a bot that plays from a bot that competes. The campaign layer is about completing things; none of that applies here. Arena play is denial, control and reading an opponent.

nuance.claim: The game has strong auto-aim that reaches much further than players expect, so shots that look impossible connect and long-range fire is worth taking.
The player model twitches toward a target when auto-aim acquires it, which is a reliable signal that a shot will hit before it is fired.
Auto-aim does not acquire an unarmed player, so switching to bare hands while retreating makes an opponent aim manually and badly.
The shortest character sits below the auto-aim solution, so assisted shots pass over him while his own are unaffected. This is the reason he is house-ruled out of most serious play.
A short opponent is hit by stopping, holding aim and pulling the reticle down manually, which costs the mobility that normally keeps a player alive.
Dark-clothed characters are genuinely harder to see in unlit arenas, so character choice is a positional advantage before anyone moves.
Crouching mid-fight shrinks the target and disrupts an opponent's established aim, and costs almost nothing to do.
Leaning exposes only part of the body and returns to cover quickly, which beats stepping out and strafing in any fight around a corner.
Any consistent movement pattern is learned and led within a few seconds, so the value is in changing the pattern once an opponent adapts to it, not in the pattern itself.
Circling in both directions rather than one keeps an opponent correcting instead of tracking.
Spawn points are a fixed, small set per arena rather than random, so where an opponent reappears is predictable and can be pre-aimed or camped.
nuance.because: Every arena's setup carries a handful of explicit Spawn records -- five in Basement, Temple and Stack, seven in Complex, eight in Library and Caves -- not a randomised pool.

nuance.claim: Arenas differ substantially in how many spawns they have, which decides whether spawn denial is viable: five points can be covered, eight cannot.
nuance.because: Spawn record counts range from five to eight across the arenas.

nuance.claim: With no objectives to contest, body armour is what an arena is actually fought over; holding it is the closest thing multiplayer has to map control.
Armour returns after a delay, so the strong pattern is to take it, fight nearby, and rotate back to it rather than to roam after picking it up.
Taking armour while already healthy denies it to everyone else, which is worth more in a close match than the health it provides.
Arenas with a single armour play as one contested point, while those with three support rotation between several; this single number changes how a map is played more than its layout does.
nuance.because: Armour records per arena: one in Basement and Temple, two in Stack and Caves, three in Complex and Library.

nuance.claim: Strong players turn the radar off because it trains attention onto a corner of the screen instead of onto the arena, but they still assume opponents are using it.
In split-screen play opponents read each other's panes, so position is never actually secret and ambushes work through timing rather than concealment.
When every hit kills, armour is worthless, weapon damage stops mattering and rate of fire and first contact decide everything; the strongest weapon becomes whichever one fires soonest.
Because a single stray round is fatal, open sightlines are far more dangerous than in any other mode and routes should hug cover even when it is slower.
Whoever holds the golden gun is visibly marked to everyone else, so the mode is three players hunting one rather than a free-for-all.
The golden gun kills in one shot through any amount of armour, so contesting it at the start is worth more than any positional advantage.
Holding the gun means being hunted by everyone at once, so the holder fights from corridors and corners where only one opponent can engage at a time.
The flag carrier cannot use weapons, items or armour at all, so the mode is pure evasion for one player and pure pursuit for the rest.
Score is time spent holding the flag, so killing the carrier matters only insofar as it stops their clock and starts yours; kills are otherwise worthless.
An unarmed carrier survives longest on a circuit through the arena's tightest geometry, because pursuers cannot cut corners they cannot see around.
With only two lives each, an even trade is a real loss, so the mode rewards disengaging from fights that are merely even.
Because lives are finite, armour is worth far more here than in an unlimited-lives match and denying it is close to a win condition.
In the unarmed set no weapons or ammunition appear at all, so the entire arena reduces to movement and positioning and every pickup route is irrelevant.
Proximity mines convert every doorway and corner into a hazard, which matters more in tight arenas than any layout knowledge; routes have to change rather than merely be walked more carefully.
Remote mines are placed early and detonated later, so their value is in predicting where someone will be rather than in where they are.
The single most reliable mine placement in any arena is on the armour, because it is the one spot every player is guaranteed to return to.
Spawn points are equally reliable mine placements, and because they are few and fixed a small number of mines covers a large share of the arena's reappearances.
nuance.because: Each arena carries only five to eight fixed Spawn records.

nuance.claim: Grenades rebound off walls, floors and ceilings, so they reach positions no direct shot can and are the answer to an opponent holding a corner.
Explosive weapons are devastating in the corridor-heavy arenas and nearly self-defeating at close range, so the same set plays completely differently by map.
Some arenas are awash with ammunition and others are genuinely scarce, so how freely fire can be traded is a property of the map rather than of the weapon set.
nuance.because: AmmoBox counts run from eleven in Basement to thirty-one in Library, a near threefold spread.
